params.description: PCAP file located at Documents and Settings/Mr. Evil/interception on disk (173,372 bytes) contains HTTP traffic analysis revealing network interception evidence. Protocol hierarchy shows: 459 total frames, 166 KB total bytes. TCP traffic includes HTTP protocol with GIF images, URL-encoded forms, and text-line data. Key IP conversations captured: (1) 192.168.254.2 <-> 207.68.174.248 (117 inbound, 145 outbound frames, 97 KB total - primary conversation); (2) HTTP requests to mobile.msn.com and login.passport.net using Windows CE Pocket PC user agent (Mozilla/4.0 compatible). Captured credentials and session cookies present: MSPAuth and MSPProf cookies visible in authentication traffic to Passport/MSN services. This represents victim network traffic being monitored/intercepted by attacker at 192.168.254.2. Recovered email evidence shows captured victim credentials including MSPAuth=5vuMneQNFDh0sFVrAbKrt*q6edOGfSSmKzi3lT1CIh6FdbNq and findme69@hotmail.com email address captured in authentication traffic.

Packet capture and bulk extractor analysis reveals victim using Pocket PC device (Windows CE, Intel PXA255 processor, 240x320 display) accessing mobile.msn.com and login.passport.net services. HTTP traffic analysis shows captured authentication session data. Recovered email and RFC822 data reveals captured Passport credentials including: (1) MSPAuth session tokens (e.g., 5vuMneQNFDh0sFVrAbKrt*q6edOGfSSmKzi3lT1CIh6FdbNq, 6jjJk8xxgDPX1OTv6h0F3ydIbK), (2) Victim email address: findme69@hotmail.com captured in MSPPre cookie, (3) Additional Passport-related cookies: MSPVis, MSPRequ, MSPDom, MSPPost indicating full authentication session capture. Attacker (192.168.254.2) captured all HTTP traffic for credential theft and account takeover. These are web-based email services accessed from mobile device, making credential interception particularly valuable for account takeover attacks.

params.system_name: Forensic Counter-Analysis and Quality Audit - NIST Hacking Case
questions_addressed: Could Ethereal, Cain & Abel, Look@LAN, and Network Stumbler have been installed for legitimate network administration - assessed against tool directory organization (EXPLOITATION/ENUMERATION/FOOTPRINTING) and actual execution evidence - conclusion: extremely unlikely given combination with malware like SAMdump and NetBus RAT

Is the Mr. Evil/Greg Schardt link definitively established - verified through registry.profile evidence showing RegisteredOwner matches Winlogon DefaultUserName - conclusion: confirmed by registry evidence

Could the victim IP and attacker IP relationship represent a test network - verified PCAP shows real Microsoft Passport/MSN services accessed by victim device with captured credentials (MSPAuth tokens, findme69@hotmail.com email) - conclusion: this is real attack against real external services
Are the tools actually configured and operational - verified through UserAssist execution timeline and prefetch records showing actual execution times and counts - conclusion: confirmed operational

Does timeline show coordinated attack sequence - analyzed execution timeline and found systematic progression from reconnaissance (2004-08-26) to packet capture tool setup (2004-08-27) with specific timing - conclusion: clearly coordinated attack sequence

What evidence exists that PCAP represents real attack - verified captured credentials in bulk.rfc822 including MSPAuth session tokens and victim email address - conclusion: real interception of legitimate user credentials

Could anonymous infrastructure indicate legitimate research - analyzed with tool combination and attacker account name 'Mr. Evil' and hacking resource browsing (2600.org, majorgeeks.com) - conclusion: indicates malicious coordination
Missing IT authorization evidence - searched for authorization, work order, legitimate purpose indicators - conclusion: no evidence of legitimate authorization or IT documentation found
Mr. Evil as humorous admin account name - evaluated against behavioral evidence (anonymous remailer access, hacking resource browsing, malicious tool combination) - conclusion: unlikely legitimate

Tools in recycle bin as failed installations - verified through ClamAV/YARA detections in active directories and UserAssist execution records - conclusion: definitely actually used, not failed installations
